section.title: Rejoice and Be at Peace
section.sectionRationale: Paul brings the letter's themes of unity and joy to a practical point. He pleads with two fellow workers to be reconciled, then gives the church a cluster of commands that shape a peaceful heart: rejoice in the Lord always, let gentleness be seen, replace anxiety with thankful prayer, and dwell on what is true and lovely. The result is the peace of God guarding hearts and minds, and the God of peace being present with them.
section.thesis: Paul urges two coworkers to be reconciled, then calls the whole church to rejoice in the Lord always, to trade anxiety for thankful prayer so that the peace of God guards their hearts and minds in Christ, and to fix their thoughts on what is true and honorable, promising that the God of peace will be with them.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the plea for Euodia and Syntyche to agree in the Lord; the call to rejoice, to pray instead of worry, and the promise of the peace of God; and the summons to think on what is excellent, with the God of peace present.

units.label: Be reconciled in the Lord
units.note: help these women who labored in the gospel

verses.text: I urge Euodia and Syntyche to agree with each other in the Lord.
Yes, and I ask you, my true yokefellow, to help these women who have contended at my side for the gospel, along with Clement and the rest of my fellow workers, whose names are in the Book of Life.

units.label: Rejoice and do not be anxious
units.note: the peace of God will guard you

verses.text: {{chairo|Rejoice}} in the Lord always. I will say it again: Rejoice!
Let your {{epieikes|gentleness}} be apparent to all. The Lord is near.
Be {{merimnao|anxious}} for nothing, but in everything, by prayer and petition, with thanksgiving, present your requests to God.
And the {{eirene|peace}} of God, which surpasses all understanding, will {{phroureo|guard}} your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.

units.label: Think on these things
units.note: and the God of peace will be with you

verses.text: Finally, brothers, whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is right, whatever is pure, whatever is lovely, whatever is admirable, if anything is excellent or praiseworthy, {{logizomai|think on}} these things.
Whatever you have learned or received or heard from me, or seen in me, put it into practice. And the God of peace will be with you.

chairo.gloss: To rejoice, to be glad. The command to rejoice in the Lord always is one of the letter's heartbeats, sounded from a prison cell. This joy is not a mood dependent on circumstances but a settled gladness in the Lord Himself, available even in hardship because its source is Christ, not comfort.

epieikes.gloss: Gentleness, reasonableness, forbearance, a gracious yielding that does not insist on its own rights. Believers are to let this quality be evident to all, a fitting counsel to a church with friction, grounded in the reminder that the Lord is near and will set all things right.

merimnao.gloss: To be anxious, to worry, to be pulled apart by care. Paul commands the opposite of anxiety, not by willpower but by turning every care into prayer. Worry and thankful prayer are set against each other: what would consume us in anxiety is to be handed over to God.

eirene.gloss: Peace, wholeness, well-being, the Hebrew shalom. The peace of God is not merely a feeling but God's own settledness standing guard over the believer. It surpasses all understanding because it does not depend on circumstances making sense, but on the God who is near and in control.

phroureo.gloss: To guard, to keep watch over, a military term for a garrison protecting a city. The peace of God mounts guard over the hearts and minds of believers in Christ Jesus, like soldiers posted at the gates, holding off the assaults of anxiety and keeping the soul secure.

logizomai.gloss: To reckon, to consider, to dwell on with the mind. Paul calls believers deliberately to fill their thinking with what is true, honorable, and lovely. The mind is not neutral; what we habitually dwell on shapes the soul, so the peace of God is guarded in part by a disciplined, God-honoring thought life.

basic.context: Paul names two women, Euodia and Syntyche, who had worked hard for the gospel but were now at odds, and he pleads with them to be reconciled and asks the church to help them. Then he gives some of the most beloved commands in the Bible: rejoice in the Lord always, be gentle, stop worrying and pray about everything with thanks, and God's peace will stand guard over your heart. Finally, fill your mind with what is good and true, and the God of peace Himself will be with you.
basic.hermeneutics: These are direct, practical commands, yet each is rooted in the gospel: joy is in the Lord, peace is God's own, the standard for our thoughts is His truth. Paul is not offering self-help techniques but showing how life in Christ reshapes our relationships, our worries, and our minds.
basic.originalLanguages: Paul commands them to chairo, rejoice, in the Lord always, and to show epieikes, gentleness, to all. Do not merimnao, be anxious, but pray, and the eirene, peace, of God will phroureo, stand guard like a garrison, over your hearts. And logizomai, dwell on, whatever is true and good.
basic.typology: The peace of God that guards the heart fulfills the covenant blessing of shalom that God pledged to His people, the wholeness of life under His care. The nearness of the Lord echoes the presence of God with Israel, now realized in Christ and consummated at His coming.
basic.christ: Joy and peace here are in the Lord and in Christ Jesus. The Lord is near, both present with His people and coming soon, and it is in Christ that the peace of God guards the heart. Christ is the source of the joy that no prison can steal and the peace that no anxiety can breach.
basic.god: God is the one to whom every anxious care is brought in prayer, the giver of a peace beyond understanding, and the God of peace who promises His own presence to those who follow the pattern of the gospel. He invites His people to cast their worries on Him and pledges Himself as their guard and companion.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Peter 5:7 says cast all your anxiety on Him. Isaiah 26:3 promises perfect peace to the mind stayed on God. Matthew 6 tells disciples not to be anxious but to seek God's kingdom.
basic.oneStory: God has always meant His people to live in the peace of His presence, freed from fear. Here that promise takes practical shape in a fractured, anxious church: reconciled to one another, rejoicing in the Lord, and guarded by a peace that points to the final shalom of the new creation where the God of peace dwells with His people.

context.literary:
Chapter 4 opens with the word Therefore, and verse 1 has already given the command to stand firm, so what follows is a series of practical applications of standing. The movement is tight. Verses 2 to 3 deal with a named conflict. Verses 4 to 7 give the three actions of joy, gentleness and prayer, with a promise attached. Verses 8 to 9 turn from what the heart is to do to what the mind is to hold, and end with a second promise. Peace stands at the end of both halves, the peace of God in verse 7 and the God of peace in verse 9, so that the two promises frame the commands like brackets.

The passage uses the same vocabulary of mind as the rest of the letter. In verse 2 Paul asks the two women to think the same thing, using the verb phroneo that has run from 2:2 and 2:5 through 3:15 and 3:19. In verse 7 the guard is set over hearts and minds. In verse 8 the mind is to take account of good things. The conflict, the worry and the thought-life are all one problem of mind, and the cure is a mind in Christ.

The list of verse 8 is carefully built, with six qualities introduced by whatever and two closing with if there is anything, as if Paul ends the list by opening it wider. Verse 9 then moves from thinking to doing with four verbs, learned, received, heard and seen. Paul has gone from rejoice, to pray, to think, to practice. The letter is moving to its close, and it comes in the form of a rich, concentrated summary of the Christian life.
context.historical:
Euodia and Syntyche are named outright, and the way Paul names them tells us something about the church. Women had a recognized part in the church at Philippi from the beginning, as Lydia's household shows, Acts 16:14 to 15 and 16:40. Paul says these two contended at his side for the gospel, using the verb of fellow athletes also found in 1:27. They were not marginal. A quarrel between two leaders in a house church would have threatened the unity of the whole assembly, and Paul addresses it in public, in a letter meant to be read aloud, with each woman named.

Clement is mentioned only here, and nothing else is known of him. The book of life in verse 3 is an image from the Old Testament. In Exodus 32:32 Moses asks to be blotted out of the book that God has written, and Psalm 69:28 and Daniel 12:1 speak of those written in it. Jesus told His disciples to rejoice that their names were written in heaven, Luke 10:20.

The reference to a garrison in verse 7 would have been vivid in a Roman colony. Soldiers kept watch over cities, and Paul knew the experience from the inside: the governor in Damascus had the city secured to arrest him, 2 Corinthians 11:32, and he was himself under guard as he wrote. For a person chained to a soldier, the promise that God's peace would stand guard over a heart had a particular weight. Paul had every reason to be anxious, and he chose to write about joy.
context.canonical:
Joy in the Lord is a major theme of the Psalms, and Paul's command compresses it. The psalmists rejoice in the LORD, in His salvation, and in His presence, and the New Testament joins joy to the Spirit, Galatians 5:22, and to the Lord's coming, Philippians 3:1 and 1 Thessalonians 5:16. The command to rejoice always stands with 1 Thessalonians 5:16 to 18, which links joy, prayer and thanksgiving as God's will.

Gentleness has a clear source in the life of Jesus. Paul appeals to the mildness and gentleness of Christ in 2 Corinthians 10:1, and he lists the same quality among the traits of a good leader and of any believer, Titus 3:2.

The prohibition of worry draws on the teaching of Jesus in Matthew 6:25 to 34, where birds and lilies show the Father's care, and on the Psalms, where burdens are to be cast on the LORD, Psalm 55:22, and where the pouring out of the heart before God is invited, Psalm 62:8. The peace of verse 7 belongs to a large thread that runs from the blessing of Numbers 6:24 to 26, through Isaiah 26:3, to the promise of Jesus in John 14:27. God is called the God of peace in Romans 15:33, Romans 16:20, 1 Thessalonians 5:23 and Hebrews 13:20. Paul closes this section with the same title, so the God who gives peace is also the God who is peace's source. The list of virtues in verse 8 can be compared with the fruit of the Spirit in Galatians 5:22 to 23 and with Romans 12:2, where renewal of the mind is the way to discern God's will.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul meant these commands to be the way a gospel-formed church lives in conflict, anxiety and temptation. He chose to deal with the quarrel first, because anxiety and disunity are linked: people who feel unsafe turn on each other. The remedy is a church where a third person helps, where the conflict is brought into the light, and where both women are reminded that their names are in the book of life.

The instruction about worry is meant to be practiced, not admired. Paul gives a method: bring everything to God, name it as a request, and do so with thanks. He does not promise that circumstances change; he promises that the heart is guarded. That is a realistic promise for a man in chains writing to a church under pressure.

The call to think on good things is a call to a disciplined mind. Paul assumes believers can choose what to dwell on and that their thinking shapes their living. He ends with his own life as evidence, telling them to practice what they have seen in him, since his example was part of the teaching. The first hearers were meant to leave with a concrete plan for a Tuesday afternoon as well as a doctrine of peace.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: Nearly everything in this passage is prescription, and it applies to every Christian. The request to Euodia and Syntyche is a particular instance, but it models the general principle that reconciliation within the church is to be pursued and helped. The promises in verses 7 and 9 are not conditions but results, and it matters how they are phrased: the peace of God will guard, and the God of peace will be with you. These describe what God does; they are not a reward for flawless technique. We should not read verse 6 as a guarantee that prayer will remove every problem, or verse 8 as permission to ignore hard realities. Paul himself wrote this from prison, honestly, with both the weight and the joy. The list of verse 8 is not an instruction to avoid difficult subjects, but to give the mind's best attention to what deserves it.

debates.question: Does Be anxious for nothing forbid all concern or care?

views.label: It forbids faithless worry, not godly concern
views.case: Paul opposes anxiety to thankful prayer; the remedy is entrusting cares to God, not suppressing all concern. Legitimate care that drives us to prayer is transformed, not condemned.

views.label: It commands the total absence of all feeling
views.case: Read as a ban on all concern, it becomes crushing and unreal; Paul himself felt daily concern for the churches. The point is to convert anxiety into prayer, not to feel nothing.

debates.bearing: The command frees believers from corrosive worry by redirecting every care to God in prayer, replacing anxiety with trust and thanksgiving.

debates.question: What is the peace that surpasses all understanding, and how does it come?

views.label: God's own peace guarding the heart
views.case: It is not merely inner calm we generate but the peace of God Himself, given to those who pray, standing guard like a garrison over heart and mind in Christ Jesus.

views.label: A technique for managing emotions
views.case: Reducing it to a self-help method misses that it is God's gift, surpassing understanding, granted through prayer and rooted in Christ, not manufactured by human effort.

debates.bearing: The peace is God's gift received through prayerful trust; it guards the believer precisely because its source and guarantee is God, not our circumstances or willpower.

debates.question: Who is the 'true yokefellow' Paul asks to help Euodia and Syntyche?

views.label: An unnamed faithful companion in Philippi
views.case: The Greek word for yokefellow is a title that Paul leaves unspelled, and he trusts the church to know who is meant. The adjective true suggests someone whose character was proven, such as Epaphroditus, who was to carry the letter, or a leader of the local church.

views.label: A proper name, Syzygus
views.case: The Greek word is also a possible personal name, and Paul may be playing on it, true Syzygus, true yokemate. Nothing else in the New Testament names such a person, so this stays a possibility.

views.label: A fellow worker such as Timothy, Luke or Silas
views.case: Some have proposed one of Paul's known companions. The letter gives no hint, and since Timothy is named alongside Paul in 1:1 and discussed in chapter 2, he is the less likely choice.

debates.bearing: The identity cannot be settled, and the passage does not need it. What matters is the request itself: a settled member of the church is asked to walk alongside two women in conflict, a model of mediation by the community and not by the apostle alone.

study.originalLanguages:
The verb in verse 4, chairo, is a present imperative, and the present tense in Greek suggests continuing action, keep rejoicing. The phrase in the Lord gives the sphere, since the joy is not in circumstances. Paul has used the same verb of his own joy in 1:18, 2:17 and 4:10, so he is asking the church to do what he has been doing in a prison.

The noun epieikes in verse 5 means gentleness, reasonableness or willingness to yield, and the abstract noun is the one Paul uses of Christ in 2 Corinthians 10:1. It describes someone who does not insist on every right. The phrase to all people widens it beyond the church. The phrase the Lord is near uses eggys, an adverb that can be either spatial or temporal, and Paul's wording allows both senses, which is why it is debated.

In verse 6 the verb merimnao, to be anxious, is the same verb Paul used of Timothy in 2:20, who will 'genuinely care' for the Philippians' needs. The word is therefore not always bad; it names a care that occupies the mind, and what matters is whether that care is carried to God. The same verb is used by Jesus in Matthew 6:25 and of Martha in Luke 10:41. Paul names four kinds of prayer in the same breath, proseuche, prayer in general, deesis, petition, aitema, specific requests, and eucharistia, thanksgiving. The first is the habit of speaking to God, the second the sense of need, the third the particular items, and the last the setting for the others.

The noun eirene in verse 7 is the Greek counterpart of the Hebrew shalom, a word of wholeness and well-being and not just quiet. The verb hyperecho, to surpass, is a compound meaning to stand above, and Paul uses it of the peace in relation to nous, a word for mind or understanding. The verb phroureo, to guard, is a military word for keeping watch as a garrison does. The same verb is used in 2 Corinthians 11:32 of the guard at Damascus and in 1 Peter 1:5 of believers being shielded by God's power. Paul does not say it will remove anxiety but that it will stand at the door of hearts and minds, kardias and noemata, the seat of will and the products of thought.

In verse 8 the first four adjectives are alethe, true, semna, honorable, dikaia, right, and hagna, pure. The following ones are prosphile, lovely, euphema, well spoken of, arete, excellence, and epainos, praise. Arete and epainos were common in Greek moral thought, and Paul borrows them without embarrassment. The verb logizomai, think on, means to reckon or take into account, the accountant's word he used of credit in Romans 4:3.

typology.fulfillment: The priests were to bless Israel with the words, may the LORD lift up His countenance toward you and give you peace, Numbers 6:26. Shalom was a gift that came from God through the priestly mouth. In Christ the gift is made personal and constant, because the peace of God guards hearts in Christ Jesus, verse 7, and He Himself says He gives a peace the world does not give, John 14:27. The escalation is from a blessing spoken over the people from outside to a peace that stands guard within. The type falls short because the priests could only wish peace; Christ made it by His blood, Colossians 1:20.

Israel marked its distinction among the nations by the nearness of its God, Deuteronomy 4:7, and the tabernacle and temple were the place where He chose to dwell. Psalm 145:18 says the LORD is near to all who call on Him. Paul's the Lord is near says that this nearness has become a person in Christ, who dwells among believers by the Spirit and will return. The type falls short in that the temple's nearness was localized and limited to a few, while Christ's nearness is to every believer, and will be complete when God dwells with His people, Revelation 21:3.

The image of a book in which God records His people runs from Moses' plea in Exodus 32:32 through Daniel 12:1 to Luke 10:20 and Revelation 3:5. In Exodus Moses offers to be blotted out for the people; in Christ the Mediator was in fact cut off for them, and names are secure in Him. Paul puts Euodia, Syntyche, Clement and the others in the book, and this is why their quarrel is not the last word. The type falls short because it is a picture, and Revelation says the names of the conquerors will never be blotted out, but it is the Lamb who holds the book, Revelation 21:27.

study.christ:
Christ is named at the center of the passage, and the center is the phrase in Christ Jesus. Verse 7 says that God's peace will guard hearts and minds in Christ Jesus, which means that the guard is posted in a place, the union with Him. The believer's mind and heart are not defended by technique but by belonging. This is why Paul also tells Euodia and Syntyche to agree in the Lord, which is the other half of the same idea. The quarrel can be settled in Him.

Christ is the source and the pattern of the commands. He is the one whose gentleness Paul invokes in 2 Corinthians 10:1, a meekness that did not defend itself, and in His Passion He showed the gentleness the passage calls for, 1 Peter 2:23. He is also the source of the peace that is not the world's, as He said in John 14:27, and the Prince of Peace of Isaiah 9:6. His blood made peace, Colossians 1:20, and by it those once far off have been brought near, Ephesians 2:13 to 17. The peace that guards the heart is therefore the result of a peace already made between God and His people at the cross.

The Lord who is near is also the Lord who will come. The nearness Paul has in mind includes the hope of His appearing, which he spoke of in 3:20, and the first Christians called out Maranatha, Come, O Lord, 1 Corinthians 16:22. That nearness changes anxiety, because the Lord is both present and approaching. Christ is also the answer to the call to think on what is true, honorable and lovely. John 14:6 gives Him as the truth, and He is the fullest case of every quality in the list. The mind that dwells on Him is the mind that does what verse 8 asks.

He is also the one whose example Paul has set before the church in chapter 2 and who provides the pattern for verse 9. The Philippians are to practice what they have seen in Paul, and Paul in turn imitates Christ, 1 Corinthians 11:1. In Gethsemane Christ Himself prayed with distress and brought His request to the Father, Matthew 26:39, which shows that prayer with petition is not a lack of faith. He gave thanks before the cross, Luke 22:19, and the pattern of thankful requests has been walked by Him.
study.god:
The passage speaks of God as the one who can be approached. The command to present requests to God assumes a God who hears, who cares about specifics, and who welcomes prayer with thanksgiving. This is the God of Psalm 145:18, who is near to all who call on Him, and of Hebrews 4:16, who invites us to the throne of grace with confidence. The anxious are not told to stop caring but to bring their care to the Person who cares, and 1 Peter 5:7 gives the reason, that He cares for us.

He is the God of peace, and the title appears twice in the passage in different forms. In verse 7 it is the peace of God, a gift that comes from Him, and in verse 9 it is the God of peace, the Person who is with His people. The first is an experience and the second a presence. Paul does not offer a feeling without the one who gives it. The peace is said to surpass understanding, which means that it cannot be calculated or explained from the circumstances, so its source must lie outside them.

He acts as a guard. The picture of a garrison shows His protection as active and not passive: He stands at the gate of the heart and mind. That does not mean He prevents all trouble, but that nothing reaches the center without His permission. That is why the believer can be in chains and yet at peace. The promise is the one in 1 Peter 1:5, that believers are shielded by God's power.

God is also the one who disciplines the mind by giving it worthy things to dwell on. The qualities of verse 8 are not arbitrary; they reflect His own character. What is true, right, pure and lovely finds its source in Him, and the believer who dwells on them is drawn toward Him. God has made a world with beauty and a Scripture with truth, and both are to be received with gratitude.

For worship, the passage teaches that joy is a duty and a gift at once. God commands rejoicing, and He supplies the reason. A people who bring their requests with thanks, who forgive and are gentle, and who find rest are doing something worship has always done: declaring that God is trustworthy.

crossReferences.note: Paul says Timothy will genuinely care for the Philippians' needs, using the same verb he forbids in 4:6 as anxious. The overlap shows that Paul is not against concern as such but against the kind of care that is cut off from God. The same word names a virtue and a vice depending on where it is carried.

Jesus tells His disciples not to worry about life, food or clothing, because the Father feeds the birds and clothes the lilies. It is the background of verse 6, and it grounds the command in the character of a heavenly Father who knows what His children need, adding that the kingdom comes first.

The LORD keeps in perfect peace the steadfast of mind who trusts in Him. The link between a settled mind and trust is the same one Paul draws in verses 6 to 8. Isaiah says that peace is the fruit of a mind fixed on God, which is why Paul turns from prayer to thought.

Cast all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you. This is the shortest version of verse 6. It gives the ground of the invitation, which is God's care, and it uses the same word for anxiety, so the two texts interpret each other.

Jesus leaves His peace with the disciples and says it is not as the world gives. It shows that the peace of God in verse 7 is the peace of Christ, spoken before the cross by the one who was about to be troubled Himself, and then bought by that cross.

The priestly blessing ends with the LORD giving peace. The source of shalom is therefore established from the law: it is God's to give. Paul's promise that the peace of God will guard is an answer to the blessing, now fulfilled in Christ.

The LORD is near to all who call on Him in truth. It is a clear background to the Lord is near in verse 5, and it connects nearness with prayer, as verse 6 does: because He is near, requests may be brought to Him.

Let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, for to this you were called as members of one body. Here peace is tied to the community as well as the heart, which fits a passage that begins with two women in dispute and ends with peace.

Rejoice at all times, pray without ceasing, give thanks in every circumstance. This is a short parallel to Philippians 4:4 to 6, with the same three practices of joy, prayer and thanks, and it describes them as God's will in Christ Jesus.

Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind. It explains why Paul bothers about what the mind dwells on in verse 8. The renewing of the mind is the means by which believers come to understand and approve God's will.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins in a state of peace, in which humans lived at ease with God, one another and the creation. The fall broke all three: the man and woman hid from God, blamed each other, and found the ground against them. Anxiety is part of the wreckage, because a person who is not at home in the world and not sure of God's care must worry. Philippians 4 is therefore not a minor piece of advice; it is a piece of the great repair.

The promise of shalom is found throughout the Old Testament. Israel was blessed with the words of Numbers 6:24 to 26. The prophets spoke of a covenant of peace, Ezekiel 37:26, and a Prince of Peace, Isaiah 9:6, and Isaiah 32:17 says that peace is the work of righteousness. Psalm 85:10 pictures righteousness and peace kissing, and the cross is where that happened. Peace was made between God and humans by Christ's blood, Colossians 1:20, and from that peace comes the peace between estranged people, Ephesians 2:14 to 16, which is why a quarrel between two women matters so much.

The church is the new community in which the repair has begun. It is a place where people who were divided are told to agree in the Lord, where anxieties are carried to God in prayer, and where minds are being renewed. It is the foretaste of a larger restoration, and its imperfections, like the quarrel in Philippi, show how much is still to be done.

The end is the new creation, where the God of peace dwells with His people. Revelation 21:3 to 4 says God will be with them and wipe every tear from their eyes. In that city nothing will need guarding because nothing will threaten, and the peace that now stands at the gate of the heart will have no enemy left to keep out. The Lord who is near will be nearer than ever, and the joy Paul commands will be unbroken.

quiz.q: What does Paul ask of Euodia and Syntyche?

options.text: To agree with each other in the Lord, with the church's help.
options.note: Verses 2 to 3 plead for their reconciliation and ask others to help.

options.text: To each prove the other one wrong.
options.note: Paul seeks agreement in the Lord, not winning an argument.

options.text: To leave the church to keep the peace.
options.note: He honors them as coworkers and calls for reconciliation, not departure.

options.text: To ignore their disagreement entirely.
options.note: He addresses it directly and asks for help to resolve it.

quiz.q: What is Paul's remedy for anxiety?

options.text: Prayer and petition with thanksgiving, bringing every request to God.
options.note: Verse 6 replaces anxiety with thankful prayer to God.

options.text: Trying harder to stop worrying by willpower.
options.note: The remedy is prayer that entrusts cares to God, not sheer willpower.

options.text: Ignoring problems until they go away.
options.note: Paul says bring everything to God, not ignore it.

options.text: Pretending everything is fine.
options.note: He invites honest requests to God, not pretense.

quiz.q: What does the peace of God do, according to verse 7?

options.text: It guards our hearts and minds in Christ Jesus.
options.note: Verse 7 says God's peace, surpassing understanding, guards heart and mind.

options.text: It removes every hardship from our lives.
options.note: It guards the heart amid hardship rather than removing all hardship.

options.text: It depends on our circumstances making sense.
options.note: It surpasses understanding, not needing circumstances to make sense.

options.text: It is a peace we manufacture ourselves.
options.note: It is the peace of God, His gift, not self-produced.

quiz.q: What are believers to fill their minds with?

options.text: Whatever is true, honorable, right, pure, lovely, and admirable.
options.note: Verse 8 lists the excellent things to dwell on.

options.text: Whatever is entertaining, regardless of its worth.
options.note: The list is about what is true and praiseworthy, not mere entertainment.

options.text: Their worries, examined over and over.
options.note: Paul redirects the mind from anxiety to what is good and true.

options.text: Nothing; the mind should stay empty.
options.note: He commands deliberate thinking on excellent things.

quiz.q: What is promised to those who practice what Paul taught?

options.text: The God of peace will be with them.
options.note: Verse 9 promises the presence of the God of peace.

options.text: A life free of all difficulty.
options.note: The promise is God's presence, not the absence of difficulty.

options.text: Immediate wealth and success.
options.note: The promise is the God of peace Himself, not material reward.

options.text: Nothing in particular.
options.note: Paul gives a clear promise, the God of peace with them.

questions: Paul urged two faithful coworkers to be reconciled. Is there a relationship where God is calling you to seek agreement in the Lord?
Paul commands joy in the Lord always, even from prison. Where do you need a joy that rests in Christ rather than in your circumstances?
Paul's answer to anxiety is thankful prayer about everything. What worry could you hand over to God in prayer right now?
The peace of God is said to guard the heart like a garrison. Where do you long for that peace to stand watch over your fears?
What we dwell on shapes us. What habits of thought might you change to fill your mind with what is true and lovely?

translationNotes.note: True yokefellow renders a phrase the BSB footnotes as possibly a proper name, loyal Syzygus; either way Paul enlists a trusted partner to help reconcile the two women.
Guard translates phroureo, a military term for a garrison keeping watch; the peace of God stands sentry over the believer's heart and mind in Christ.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched from bible.helloao.org for Philippians 4:2-9 this session. wording is unchanged.
